title: Best word each time, best sentence?
hook: Always pick the likeliest next word. Do you end up with the likeliest sentence?

knows: that a language model gives each possible next word a chance
doesNotKnow: that a sentence's chance is the product of its words' chances
that taking the likeliest word at each step can miss the likeliest sentence

misconception: Taking the most likely word at each step gives the most likely text.
objective: The learner can explain that a sentence's chance is the product along its path, so a less likely first word can lead to a more likely whole sentence than the greedy choice.

claims.text: Greedy takes 'cat' (60%) then 'sat' (40%): 0.6 × 0.4 = 24%. 'dog' (40%) then 'barked' (90%) gives 0.4 × 0.9 = 36%, the most likely two-word ending in the tree.
claims.source: GREEDY_P and OTHER_P in Demo.tsx; node: 0.24, 0.36. Other leaves: cat ran 21%, cat ate 15%, dog sat 4%.

claims.text: A sentence's chance is the product of each word's chance given the words before it.
claims.source: Chain rule of probability: P(w1, w2) = P(w1) · P(w2 | w1). Standard for autoregressive language models, e.g. Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed. draft), ch. 3.

claims.text: The words and their odds are invented, labelled 'Invented word odds' on the stage.
claims.source: Brief 40 in company/domains/briefs/ai.md (A/B with 60/40, best-next 40% and 90%); words added for readability.

claims.text: Some real systems use beam search, keeping several partial sentences at each step, to get closer to the most likely whole sentence than greedy picking.
claims.source: About real systems: Sutskever, Vinyals & Le 2014, 'Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks', NeurIPS (left-to-right beam search keeping B partial hypotheses); beam search is an approximation, not guaranteed to find the best sequence.

recall.question: A text generator always picks the single likeliest next word. Why can the sentence it produces be less likely than another one?
options: A strong first word can lead to weak next words; the sentence's chance multiplies along the way
Because the likeliest word is always wrong
It cannot: the likeliest words always make the likeliest sentence
recall.why: A sentence's chance is the product of its words' chances. A slightly less likely first word can open up a near-certain next word and win overall.
